title: Instruction Fine-Tuning
blurb: Tests what instruction fine-tuning changes, why loss is computed only on the response, why quality beats quantity, LoRA and QLoRA arithmetic, chat templates and format consistency, how to evaluate a tuned model, and what six examples taught GPT-2.

ideas.title: What IFT changes and how it trains
When IFT fits and when it breaks

questions.prompt: What does a base model do with "What is the capital of France?" before instruction fine-tuning?
options: Answers "Paris", since the fact is in its weights and it was trained to help
Returns an error, because base models only accept a full document as input
Refuses, because it has no system prompt telling it to answer questions
Continues the text in whatever direction its training data suggests next
questions.explanation: A base model is a text continuation engine. It might produce more quiz questions or a Wikipedia excerpt. IFT is what teaches it to treat the message as an instruction to answer.

questions.prompt: During IFT, which part of each example is the loss computed on?
options: Only the user message, so the model learns to read instructions closely
Only the system prompt, since that sets the behaviour the model should learn
Only the assistant response, token by token, against the reference answer
The system prompt, the user message and the response, equally weighted
questions.explanation: The model isn't penalised for the system prompt or user message, only for how well it produces the response. The objective is still next-token prediction, applied to the response tokens.

questions.prompt: What did the LIMA paper show?
options: 50,000 examples beat 1,000, since IFT needs as much data as pretraining.
Quality and quantity matter equally, so a 50/50 mix of clean and noisy data works best.
IFT works only after continuous pretraining on at least a billion domain tokens.
1,000 carefully curated examples beat 50,000 lower-quality ones.
questions.explanation: For IFT, quality dominates. The model already knows how to write, and IFT teaches it which kind of writing to choose. That is the opposite of pretraining and CPT, where quantity dominates.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter separate IFT from CPT?
options: They are the same method, run on different datasets at different times.
CPT uses LoRA and IFT updates all weights.
CPT changes the tokenizer, while IFT changes only the output layer of the model.
CPT is self-supervised on raw text and changes knowledge. IFT is supervised on pairs and changes behaviour.
questions.explanation: The two have different objectives and data, not just different datasets. Both can use LoRA or full updates, and neither changes the tokenizer.

questions.prompt: How does LoRA change the forward pass of a layer with weight W?
options: It becomes (W + I)x, with the identity added so the original weights can be trained faster.
W is replaced by a rank-r copy, and the full matrix is thrown away to save memory.
It becomes Wx + BAx, with W frozen and only the small matrices A and B trained.
W is quantised to 4 bits, and its rounding errors are learned by a second network.
questions.explanation: LoRA adds a low-rank update B·A beside the frozen W. A is d × r and B is r × d, with r around 8 to 64. Quantising the base model is what QLoRA adds on top.

questions.prompt: LoRA with rank r = 16 is applied to one 4096 × 4096 projection. Using about 2 · d · r trainable parameters, how many does that add?
questions.explanation: A has 4096 × 16 and B has 16 × 4096 parameters, so 2 × 4096 × 16 = 131,072. The full matrix has about 16.8 million, so the adapter is under 1% of it.

questions.prompt: GPT-2's fused c_attn layer maps 768 inputs to 2,304 outputs. With rank 8, A is 768 × 8 and B is 8 × 2304. Across GPT-2's 12 layers, how many trainable parameters does LoRA add?
questions.explanation: Per layer: 768 × 8 + 8 × 2304 = 6,144 + 18,432 = 24,576. Times 12 layers is 294,912, the number print_trainable_parameters() reported in the worked example.

questions.prompt: QLoRA stores a 7-billion-parameter base model at 4 bits per weight. Counting only the weights, at exactly 4 bits each, how many GB do they take? Use 1 GB = 10^9 bytes.
questions.explanation: 4 bits is 0.5 bytes, and 7 × 10^9 × 0.5 = 3.5 GB. The chapter's "roughly 4 GB" allows for overheads such as quantisation constants. Either way it is down from about 14 GB in fp16.

questions.prompt: Procedure 34.3 says to call print_trainable_parameters(). What mistake does that catch?
options: Dropout set above 0.1, which the check flags because it slows LoRA training
The base model loading in fp32, which shows up as twice the expected total
A learning rate too high for LoRA, which the printout shows as a negative count
target_modules not matching the model's layer names, so far more or fewer parameters train than intended
questions.explanation: Layer names differ between architectures. GPT-2 uses c_attn, Llama uses q_proj and the rest. If the names don't match, the count is wrong, and the run trains the wrong thing without any error.

questions.prompt: Why should tokenizer.apply_chat_template() format examples at both training and serving time?
options: It removes the system prompt, which the model would otherwise be penalised for.
Any gap between training-time and serving-time formatting hurts output quality.
It is the only function that can write JSONL files in the format peft expects.
It compresses the prompt so the model fits more examples into its context window.
questions.explanation: A hand-rolled template that doesn't match the tokenizer's chat template at serving time is a common failure. One source of truth for formatting on both sides avoids it.

questions.prompt: A dataset mixes Alpaca-style rows with chat-style rows. What does Procedure 34.1 say?
options: Convert the chat rows to Alpaca, since peft only accepts the Alpaca format.
Pick one format and template every example in exactly the same way.
Keep both, since variety in format helps the model generalise to new prompts.
Keep both, but put all Alpaca rows first so the model learns them separately.
questions.explanation: Mixing formats is the procedure's common mistake. Inconsistent formatting is noise, and a small IFT set is hurt by noise the most. Variety belongs in the instructions, not the template.

questions.prompt: Which does the chapter list as signs of a high-quality IFT dataset? Select all that apply.
options: Consistent formatting and voice
Diverse instructions across task types
Accurate, complete, appropriately concise responses
Many near-duplicates of the best examples
questions.explanation: The chapter adds no contradictions and minimal repetition. Near-duplicates hurt IFT the same way they hurt CPT.

questions.prompt: Why must an IFT model be compared against its base model on the same evaluation set?
options: The comparison is required by the peft library before it will save the adapter.
The base model's scores are needed to compute the LoRA rank to use for the next training run.
Without the baseline, you can't tell real improvement from the model just becoming narrower.
Base models always score higher, so the comparison sets an upper bound on quality.
questions.explanation: IFT should improve the task while keeping general ability. A side-by-side on the same set shows both. Nothing in peft requires it, and base models don't always score higher.

questions.prompt: A model is tuned to write SQL. What task-specific metric does the chapter suggest?
options: Count how many SQL keywords appear in each generated answer.
Compute ROUGE between the generated SQL and a reference query.
Ask the tuned model itself to grade its queries from 1 to 5.
Run the generated SQL and check that the results are correct.
questions.explanation: For SQL, execution is the real test. Two different queries can both be right, so ROUGE misleads. Self-grading suffers from self-preference bias, as Chapter 32 explains.

questions.prompt: A team has 80 good examples of the output they want. What does the chapter suggest trying first?
options: Full-parameter fine-tuning, since small sets need all weights updated
Continuous pretraining on the 80 examples, repeated until loss reaches zero
Prompt engineering, since under about 200 examples it is usually the better first move
QLoRA, since small datasets need 4-bit quantisation to avoid overfitting
questions.explanation: The trade-offs section says IFT works with roughly 500 to 100,000 good pairs, and below about 200, prompting is usually better. Quantisation doesn't prevent overfitting, and CPT needs millions of tokens.

questions.prompt: A company wants its assistant to know this quarter's new product prices. Is IFT the right tool?
options: Yes, if the prices are written as instruction and response pairs with a strict template.
No. IFT memorises facts poorly. RAG is the right tool for factual grounding.
No. Only full retraining from scratch can add facts to a model after its release.
Yes. IFT is the standard way to add new facts, as long as the format is consistent.
questions.explanation: The chapter says IFT breaks down on tasks needing new facts. RAG grounds answers in current data. Changing knowledge in the weights is CPT's job, and that suits large domains, not a price list.

questions.prompt: Half of a team's training responses are terse and half are chatty. What will IFT learn?
options: The inconsistency, as faithfully as it would learn a consistent pattern
The terse style, since shorter answers have lower loss per example
Neither style, since inconsistent data stops training from converging at all
The average of the two styles, which comes out medium length
questions.explanation: The chapter warns that the model learns inconsistency as faithfully as the pattern. You get both styles, unpredictably. Training still converges, it just converges on mixed behaviour.

questions.prompt: The worked example reports 294,912 trainable parameters out of 124,734,720. What percentage trains? Give two decimal places.
questions.explanation: 294,912 / 124,734,720 = 0.00236, or 0.24%. That sits inside the chapter's 0.1–1% range.

questions.prompt: After training on six examples, what did GPT-2 produce for the held-out "What is the capital of Portugal?"
options: A wrong answer, Madrid, copied from one of the training examples it had memorised
A clean, single-line answer, "Lisbon.", with no artefacts
The right answer, Lisbon, followed by a repeated "Response:" artefact
The same loop as before training, "The capital of Portugal is the capital of Portugal."
questions.explanation: The output was "Lisbon. Response: Lisbon. Response: Portugal." The model generalised the answer to a new country, but the tiny set didn't teach clean formatting. The loop was the before-training output.

questions.prompt: Training loss went 0.265 at epoch 20, then 0.539, then 0.415. How does the chapter read this?
options: The run is broken, and the weights from epoch 20 onward should be treated as corrupted.
It shows catastrophic forgetting of the base model's knowledge about capitals.
It oscillates near its minimum, a normal effect of six examples and full-batch updates.
It proves the learning rate was too low for the model to reach a real minimum.
questions.explanation: With six examples, full-batch updates and a fairly high LoRA learning rate, loss bounces near its minimum. The chapter calls this a realistic artefact, not a broken run. A rate that was too low would not oscillate like this.

questions.prompt: The chapter says the tuned model learned no new facts about capitals. What did it learn?
options: The fact that Lisbon is Portugal's capital, from a hidden seventh example
To express knowledge it already had, in the trained response format
Every capital of the world, from patterns in the six country names it saw
Nothing at all. The right answer was a lucky guess from random weights.
questions.explanation: IFT changes behaviour, not knowledge. The fact was already latent in GPT-2's weights, and the six examples taught it to answer in the "Response: Y." pattern. That is the chapter's CPT-versus-IFT distinction in one example.

bookExercises.prompt: State the three parts of an IFT training example, and explain which part(s) loss is computed on during training.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The three parts: system prompt, user message, assistant response. Loss is computed only on the assistant response. The model isn't penalised for how it represents the system prompt or user message, only for how well it produces the correct response given them.

bookExercises.prompt: Write LoRA's effective forward-pass formula ($W \cdot x + B \cdot A \cdot x$) and state which of $W$, $A$, $B$ are frozen versus trained.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `W·x + B·A·x`. `W` (the base model's original weight matrix) is frozen. `A` and `B` (the low-rank adapter matrices) are the only trained parameters.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 34.4's measured trainable-parameter count (294,912 of 124,734,720, or 0.2364%), explain why this figure falling within Exposition's stated "0.1–1%" range is a meaningful sanity check, not just a confirmation of something already known. What would a figure of, say, 40% have indicated about the `target_modules` configuration?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The trainable-parameter percentage falling inside the expected 0.1–1% range confirms that `target_modules=["c_attn"]` correctly matched real layers in the model and that LoRA is doing what it's supposed to: adapting a small slice of the architecture rather than accidentally leaving the base model fully trainable or matching nothing at all. A figure of 40% would indicate `target_modules` matched far more of the model than intended (or LoRA wasn't actually restricting training to adapters), effectively defeating LoRA's entire memory/compute advantage while still reporting as "using LoRA": exactly the kind of silent misconfiguration the `print_trainable_parameters()` sanity check exists to catch before an expensive training run.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's before/after generations for "capital of Portugal," identify specifically which part of the output demonstrates genuine generalisation and which part demonstrates a training-set-size artifact, and explain why both can be true of the same generated output.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The genuine generalisation is producing "Lisbon," the correct answer to a question about a country (Portugal) that never appeared in any of the six training examples, meaning the model correctly extended the learned instruction-response pattern to a held-out case. The training-set-size artifact is the trailing repetition, "Response: Lisbon. Response: Portugal.", a malformed continuation pattern not present in any training example, which is exactly the kind of instability six examples (far below even LIMA's 1,000-example floor) would be expected to produce. Both can be true simultaneously because they reflect different aspects of what was learned. The semantic mapping (country → capital) generalised well from a small, consistent pattern, while the precise boundary of "when to stop generating" is a subtler formatting behavior that needed more examples to stabilise.

bookExercises.prompt: A team wants to fine-tune a model to know their company's Q3 financial results. Using this chapter's Trade-offs section and Motivation, write the two or three sentences you'd say about why IFT is the wrong tool for this and what to use instead.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "IFT teaches a model how to communicate, not new fixed facts. It memorises poorly, and any facts baked in this way go stale the moment next quarter's results are released. For quarterly financial results specifically, use RAG (Chapter 31): index the actual results documents and let the model retrieve and cite them at query time. That's also auditable. You can show exactly which document backed an answer, which a fine-tuned model's baked-in 'knowledge' cannot."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 34.2 warns about mismatched chat templates between training and serving. Describe a concrete way this mismatch could pass unit tests but still degrade quality in production, using this chapter's description of what a chat template controls.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A team could fine-tune a model using a hand-written prompt template that superficially resembles the model's expected chat format (e.g., manually writing `[INST]...[/INST]` tags) and pass all training-time tests, since the training loop only checks that loss decreases on the hand-formatted examples. If the exact special tokens, whitespace, or tag placement differ even slightly from what `tokenizer.apply_chat_template()` produces at serving time, the served model receives inputs formatted differently from what it was trained on. That degrades output quality in production even though every training-time unit test (which never exercised the actual serving-time template) passed cleanly.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about QLoRA's 4-bit quantisation (NF4) approach. Explain in your own words why quantising the *frozen* base model weights, while keeping the LoRA adapters themselves in higher precision, is a reasonable design choice rather than quantising everything uniformly.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Quantising only the frozen base weights to 4-bit while keeping LoRA adapters in higher precision (fp16/bf16) is reasonable because the base weights are never updated during training. They only need enough precision to produce a reasonably accurate forward pass, and 4-bit NF4 quantisation is specifically designed to preserve the statistical distribution of pretrained weights well enough for this. The LoRA adapters, by contrast, are exactly the parameters receiving gradient updates. Keeping them in higher precision avoids compounding quantisation error with the optimizer's own numerical sensitivity (small updates to already-quantized low-precision values would lose meaningful signal), so the precision budget is spent where training actually happens rather than uniformly across parameters that never change.
